text: You already know Azure RBAC assigns roles and Azure Policy enforces rules. What matters operationally is which question each one answers, because that's what tells you which tool actually fits a given governance problem.

RBAC answers: can this principal attempt this action at all? It's evaluated by Resource Manager at authorization time, before anything happens. Policy answers a different question: is this resource's configuration allowed, regardless of who created it? That's why an Owner, who can do anything RBAC permits, can still be blocked from creating an unencrypted storage account. RBAC authorized the attempt. Policy judged the result.

A role definition is scoped permission data. Actions are the management-plane operations it grants. NotActions carve exclusions out of a broader Actions wildcard — that's literally how Contributor is built, everything minus granting access to others. DataActions govern data-plane operations like reading blob contents, separately from management-plane actions. Every assignment also carries a scope, and permissions apply there and everything beneath it.

A policy definition evaluates a resource and applies an effect. Deny stops a non-compliant write entirely. Audit lets the write through but flags it non-compliant, useful for rolling out a new standard without breaking anyone immediately. AuditIfNotExists flags a missing related resource. DeployIfNotExists actually remediates, deploying that missing resource using a managed identity with its own scoped permissions. Modify adds, updates, or removes properties or tags directly at write time.

Real governance almost always needs both. Say only the platform team should create storage accounts, and every one must have public blob access disabled. The first half is RBAC: restrict that action to a custom role for the platform team. The second half is Policy, because RBAC has no concept of a storage account's public-access property. RBAC alone misses a mistake by the right people. Policy alone lets anyone attempt the creation in the first place.

RBAC restricts who can act; Policy constrains what the result is allowed to look like, and production environments layer both rather than picking one. Next lesson turns to the identities applications themselves use — service principals and managed identities — and how to secure their credentials, or avoid needing any at all.
